The smell of old books has always fascinated me. There's something about that particular scent—musty, papery, faintly sweet—that instantly transports me to another world. My grandmother's attic was filled with them: leather-bound volumes, dog-eared paperbacks, encyclopedias with cracked spines. I used to spend summer afternoons up there, lying on a worn velvet armchair, completely lost in stories.

Now, decades later, I still find myself drawn to used bookstores. The moment I push open that heavy door, breathing in that familiar aroma, I feel like I'm coming home. There's a particular shop downtown that I visit every few months. The owner knows me by name and always has recommendations ready.

Last weekend, I found a first edition of a novel I'd loved as a teenager. The pages were yellowed, the cover faded, but holding it felt like reuniting with an old friend. I brought it home, made a cup of tea, and settled into my reading chair. The afternoon light filtered through the window as I turned the first page, and for a moment, I was twelve years old again, sprawled in my grandmother's attic, believing anything was possible.

Books have this magic—they hold time. They preserve not just the stories within their pages, but the moments we shared with them, the people we were when we first read them. Every cracked spine carries history, every dog-eared corner marks a memory. In a world that moves so fast, there's something deeply comforting about that kind of permanence.
